mcqs.question: In a bounded-buffer solution with multiple producer threads, why is a separate mutex still needed even though counting semaphores already track empty/full slots?
options: It isn't needed — the counting semaphores alone are sufficient with multiple producers
The mutex is only needed for portability across operating systems
Without it, two producers could race on the same buffer insertion index and corrupt the buffer's internal state
The mutex replaces the need for counting semaphores entirely
mcqs.explanation: The counting semaphores only track how many slots are available, not who's allowed to touch the buffer's internal pointers at a given instant — with multiple producers, two could otherwise both pass their empty-slot check and then race writing to the same index. The mutex and the semaphores do genuinely different jobs; neither replaces the other, and this has nothing to do with portability.

mcqs.question: In the first (readers-priority) readers-writers solution, what causes writer starvation?
options: The main lock has a bug that never actually grants access to writers
The solution doesn't allow more than one reader at a time, so writers wait behind a queue of single readers
Writers are given lower thread priority by the operating system scheduler
As long as read_count never drops to zero, a waiting writer never gets the lock, since readers keep the lock held indefinitely
mcqs.explanation: The bug is structural, not a scheduler priority issue: as long as a continuous stream of readers keeps read_count above zero, the resource lock stays held by readers and a waiting writer never gets a turn. This solution deliberately allows unlimited concurrent readers (that's the point), which is exactly what enables the starvation.

mcqs.question: The writers-preference fix to readers-writers blocks new readers from starting once a writer is waiting. What new problem can this introduce?
options: It can cause a deadlock between readers and writers
It has no downside — it strictly improves on the first solution
It makes concurrent reads unsafe
It can starve readers if writers arrive back-to-back continuously
mcqs.explanation: Giving writers preference fixes writer starvation but flips the risk: if writers keep arriving before the queue ever empties, readers can be perpetually blocked. There's no deadlock introduced and concurrent reads remain safe when they do run — it's a fairness trade-off, not a strict improvement with no cost.

mcqs.question: What do the resource-ordering, arbitrator, and odd/even solutions to dining philosophers all have in common?
options: They all add a sixth fork to the table
They all rely on a central deadlock detector to abort a philosopher
They all remove the need for mutual exclusion on the forks
They all break the circular wait that lets all philosophers deadlock in lockstep
mcqs.explanation: All three solutions work by structurally preventing the circular chain of waiting that causes deadlock — via ordering, via limiting concurrent attempts, or via alternating pickup order — none add extra resources, remove mutual exclusion (each fork still needs exclusive use), or depend on detection-and-abort after the fact.

mcqs.question: Two application code paths each acquire locks A and B, but in opposite order (one does A then B, the other does B then A). What is the most robust fix?
options: Add a timeout to every lock acquisition and hope it resolves itself
Establish and enforce a single global lock ordering across the whole codebase, so every path acquires shared locks in the same order
Switch both locks to spinlocks
Add more logging so the deadlock is easier to see after it happens
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the dining-philosophers circular-wait shape applied to two locks; the structural fix is a consistent, codebase-wide lock ordering so no two code paths can ever acquire the same locks in opposite order. Timeouts can mask the symptom without preventing it, changing lock type doesn't address ordering, and logging only helps diagnose after the fact, not prevent it.
